claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Loss of OCT4-dependent chromatin accessibility and transcription factor binding was broadly associated with the down-regulation of nearby genes.
claims.source: To understand whether this loss of combinatorial transcription factor binding was relevant to gene regulation, we carried out nuclear RNA-seq in wild type and OCT4-depleted cells. Loss of OCT4-dependent chromatin accessibility and transcription factor binding was broadly associated with the down-regulation of nearby genes (Figure 2C–E), such as the pluripotency-associated Utf1 gene (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claims.claim: 82% of genes with reduced expression near OCT4-bound distal sites showed coincident reductions in chromatin accessibility.
claims.source: When we examined this relationship across the genome, reductions in the expression of genes near OCT4-bound distal sites was highly coincident (82%) with reductions in chromatin accessibility (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Genes that were down-regulated in OCT4-depleted ESCs tended to be significantly closer to OCT4 binding sites that displayed reduced chromatin accessibility (median distance 16.2 kb) than OCT4 binding sites that retained chromatin accessibility (median distance 125.4 kb).
claims.source: Nevertheless, genes that were down-regulated in OCT4-depleted ESCs (n = 1430; OCT4-dependent gene expression) tended to be significantly closer to OCT4 binding sites that displayed reduced chromatin accessibility (median distance 16.2 kb) than OCT4 binding sites that retained chromatin accessibility in the absence of OCT4 (median distance 125.4 kb) (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Genes down-regulated after loss of OCT4 are enriched for the pluripotency transcriptional network.
claims.source: These sites were also characterized by reductions in SOX2 and NANOG binding (Figure 2A,B) and their associated genes were enriched for the pluripotency-associated transcriptional network (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Of nine individual chromatin remodelling complexes examined, only BRG1 showed an appreciable correlation between occupancy and the reliance on OCT4 for chromatin accessibility.
claims.source: Remarkably, of the nine individual chromatin remodelling complexes examined, only BRG1 (SMARCA4), a catalytic ATPase subunit of the vertebrate SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex (also referred to as BRG1-associated factor (BAF) remodelling complexes), showed an appreciable correlation between occupancy and the reliance on OCT4 for chromatin accessibility (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A comparing nine chromatin remodellers.

claims.claim: BRG1 was significantly enriched at regulatory elements that relied on OCT4 for chromatin accessibility.
claims.source: Indeed, BRG1 was significantly enriched at regulatory elements that relied on OCT4 for chromatin accessibility (OCT4-dependent ATAC peaks) and regulatory elements bound by OCT4 (Figure 3B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claims.claim: OCT4 and BRG1 occupancy was highly correlated throughout the mouse ESC genome.
claims.source: Furthermore, OCT4 and BRG1 occupancy was highly correlated throughout the mouse ESC genome (Figure 3E and Ho et al. (2009), Kidder et al. (2009), de Dieuleveult et al., 2016), supporting the possibility that there may be a functional link between OCT4 binding, BRG1, and chromatin accessibility.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genome-wide correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E and citations to Ho et al. (2009), Kidder et al. (2009), and de Dieuleveult et al., 2016.

claims.claim: BRG1 is essential for maintaining ESC pluripotency.
claims.source: BRG1, like OCT4, is essential for maintaining ESC pluripotency (Ho et al., 2009; Kidder et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014), supporting early embryonic development (Bultman et al., 2006) and improving the efficiency of iPSC reprogramming (Singhal et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2009; Kidder et al., 2009; and Zhang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: BRG1 supports early embryonic development.
claims.source: BRG1, like OCT4, is essential for maintaining ESC pluripotency (Ho et al., 2009; Kidder et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014), supporting early embryonic development (Bultman et al., 2006) and improving the efficiency of iPSC reprogramming (Singhal et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Bultman et al., 2006.

claims.claim: BRG1 improves the efficiency of iPSC reprogramming.
claims.source: BRG1, like OCT4, is essential for maintaining ESC pluripotency (Ho et al., 2009; Kidder et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014), supporting early embryonic development (Bultman et al., 2006) and improving the efficiency of iPSC reprogramming (Singhal et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Singhal et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Chromatin accessibility was reduced at the majority of OCT4-bound sites following BRG1 depletion.
claims.source: When we extended this analysis to all OCT4-bound sites, it was clear that chromatin accessibility was reduced (Figure 3I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and nucleosome occupancy increased following BRG1 depletion at the majority of OCT4 target sites (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Nucleosome occupancy increased following BRG1 depletion at the majority of OCT4 target sites.
claims.source: When we extended this analysis to all OCT4-bound sites, it was clear that chromatin accessibility was reduced (Figure 3I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and nucleosome occupancy increased following BRG1 depletion at the majority of OCT4 target sites (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by nucleosome occupancy data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: 45% of OCT4-bound sites showed significantly reduced ATAC-seq signal following BRG1 removal using a stringent threshold (fold change >1.5 and FDR < 0.05).
claims.source: We then used a stringent threshold (fold change >1.5 and FDR < 0.05) to identify sites that experienced significant reductions in chromatin accessibility following BRG1 removal. This revealed that 45% of OCT4-bound sites showed significantly reduced ATAC-seq signal and these sites were also highly dependent on OCT4 for their accessibility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential binding analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: 76% of OCT4-bound sites that rely on OCT4 for their accessibility were also dependent on BRG1 for their accessibility.
claims.source: Indeed, when we applied an unbiased clustering approach to examine the relationship between removal of OCT4 and BRG1 in shaping accessibility it was clear that the majority (76%) of OCT4-bound sites that rely on OCT4 for their accessibility were also dependent on BRG1 for their accessibility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Loss of either OCT4 or BRG1 resulted in similar reductions in chromatin accessibility across nearly all OCT4 peaks.
claims.source: Importantly, the loss of either OCT4 or BRG1 appeared to result in similar, although not identical, reductions in chromatin accessibility across nearly all OCT4 peaks (Figure 3I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), revealing that both of these factors are required to maintain chromatin accessibility at these loci in mouse ESCs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of ATAC-seq changes shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Large scale proteomic studies have indicated that BRG1 may interact physically with OCT4.
claims.source: Given that large scale proteomic studies have previously indicated that BRG1 may interact physically with OCT4 (Pardo et al., 2010; van den Berg et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2012), and BRG1 is enriched at OCT4-bound sites throughout the genome (Figure 3), we favoured the possibility that OCT4 recruits BRG1 and the associated BAF complex to OCT4 target sites in the genome in order to remodel chromatin and promote chromatin accessibility.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Pardo et al., 2010; van den Berg et al., 2010; and Ding et al., 2012.

claims.claim: OCT4, BRG1 and SS18 are enriched within the nucleosome-depleted region at OCT4 target sites.
claims.source: In fitting with this possibility, OCT4, BRG1 and the additional BAF subunit, SS18, are enriched within the nucleosome-depleted region at OCT4 target sites (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by high-resolution metaplot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: A dramatic reduction in BRG1 and SS18 binding at OCT4 target sites was observed in the absence of OCT4.
claims.source: Although BRG1 and SS18 protein levels were unaffected following removal of OCT4 (Figure 1A), we observed a dramatic reduction in BRG1 and SS18 binding at OCT4 target sites in the absence of OCT4 (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data for BRG1 and SS18 shown in Figure 4B,C and protein levels shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Loss of BRG1 and SS18 at OCT4 binding sites was specific to OCT4-bound regulatory elements as regulatory elements lacking OCT4 were unaffected.
claims.source: This loss was specific to OCT4-bound regulatory elements as regulatory elements lacking OCT4 were unaffected (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4D comparing OCT4-bound and OCT4-free sites.

claims.claim: There was a good correlation between the loss of BRG1 and SS18 and loss of ATAC-seq signal at OCT4 binding sites in OCT4-depleted ESCs.
claims.source: Indeed, when we compared reductions in chromatin accessibility with reductions in BRG1 and SS18 at OCT4 binding sites, there was a good correlation between the loss of these factors and loss of ATAC-seq signal in OCT4-depleted ESCs (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: BRG1 is recruited to pluripotency-associated enhancers coincident with the formation of accessible chromatin during iPSC reprogramming.
claims.source: Interestingly, our observation that OCT4 recruits the BRG1/BAF complex to its target sites in ESCs is in agreement with recent observations that BRG1 is recruited to pluripotency-associated enhancers coincident with the formation of accessible chromatin during iPSC reprogramming (Chronis et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chronis et al., 2017.

claims.claim: 60% of distal OCT4 targets showed significant reductions in OCT4 binding following BRG1 removal (FDR < 0.05 and fold change >1.5 fold).
claims.source: Strikingly, we observed significant reductions in OCT4 binding at the majority (60%; FDR < 0.05 and fold change >1.5 fold) of distal OCT4 targets following BRG1 removal (Figure 5A–C), indicating that BRG1 contributes not only to creating accessibility at OCT4 target sites but is also required to sustain normal OCT4 binding in mouse ESCs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claims.claim: SOX2 and NANOG binding was significantly reduced following BRG1 removal in ESCs (16.7% and 22.9% of distal OCT4 target sites; FDR < 0.05 and fold change >1.5 fold).
claims.source: Similarly, SOX2 and NANOG binding was also significantly reduced following BRG1 removal in ESCs, although the total number of sites significantly affected was less than for OCT4 (16.7% and 22.9% of distal OCT4 target sites; FDR < 0.05 and fold change >1.5 fold) (Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claims.claim: Loss of BRG1 did not result in complete loss of transcription factor binding at the most extremely affected OCT4 target sites, yet resulted in an inability of the cells to maintain the nucleosome-depleted state.
claims.source: Importantly, even when we examined the most extremely affected OCT4 target sites (BRG1-dependent), loss of BRG1 did not result in complete loss of transcription factor binding (Figure 5D), yet resulted in an inability of the cells to maintain the nucleosome-depleted state (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 5D and nucleosome occupancy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The expression of genes associated with sites that rely on BRG1 for OCT4 binding tended to be reduced following deletion of BRG1.
claims.source: Importantly, this analysis revealed that the expression of genes associated with sites that rely on BRG1 for OCT4 binding tended to be reduced following deletion of BRG1 (Figure 5E–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E-G and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Genes associated with unchanged or increased OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG binding tended to show increases in expression following BRG1 removal.
claims.source: In contrast, genes associated with unchanged or increased OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG binding tended to show increases in expression (Figure 5E–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E-G and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Distal OCT4 binding sites in close proximity to OCT4/BRG1 dependent genes experienced the largest reductions in transcription factor binding following removal of BRG1.
claims.source: Furthermore, distal OCT4 binding sites in close proximity to OCT4/BRG1 dependent genes experienced the largest reductions in transcription factor binding following removal of BRG1 (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Genes associated with BRG1-independent OCT4 binding were activated early during reprogramming and BRG1-dependent sites later.
claims.source: This revealed that genes associated with BRG1-independent OCT4 binding were activated early during reprogramming and BRG1-dependent sites later (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of reprogramming time course data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Genes that require BRG1 for OCT4 binding were expressed later during reprogramming.
claims.source: In contrast, genes that require BRG1 for OCT4 binding were expressed later during reprogramming, perhaps because OCT4 requires BRG1 at these sites to remodel chromatin and mature the function of these regulatory elements.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of reprogramming time course data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: BRG1-dependent OCT4 binding sites were associated with genes expressed at later developmental stages during early mouse development.
claims.source: In fitting with this possibility, BRG1-dependent OCT4 binding sites were also associated with genes expressed at later developmental stages during early mouse development (Figure 6B), suggesting that chromatin state in the early embryo may also shape how these OCT4 target sites are used during development.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GREAT annotation analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: BRG1-dependent OCT4 target sites became accessible at later stages of embryonic development.
claims.source: Interestingly, this demonstrated that BRG1-dependent OCT4 target sites became accessible at later stages of embryonic development (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq and DNase-seq data during early development shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: OCT4 occupies sites that would otherwise be inaccessible and is required to shape the occupancy of additional pluripotency transcription factors.
claims.source: In doing so we discover that OCT4 occupies sites that would otherwise be inaccessible and is required to shape the occupancy of additional pluripotency transcription factors.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: OCT4 achieves shaping of transcription factor occupancy by recruiting the chromatin remodelling factor BRG1 to support not only its own binding but also to stabilize further transcription factor binding events required to support pluripotency-associated gene regulation.
claims.source: OCT4 achieves this by recruiting the chromatin remodelling factor BRG1 to support not only its own binding but also to stabilize further transcription factor binding events required to support pluripotency-associated gene regulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 3-5.

claims.claim: The pioneering activities of OCT4 are required not only during reprogramming, but also in the established pluripotent state.
claims.source: This suggests that the pioneering activities of OCT4 are required not only during reprogramming, but also in the established pluripotent state.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on findings from Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: OCT4 may be able to dynamically sample its target sites throughout the genome through its capacity to bind nucleosomal DNA.
claims.source: A requirement of this process is OCT4's ability to engage with sequences in inaccessible chromatin presumably through its capacity to bind nucleosomal DNA (Figure 1; Soufi et al., 2012, 2015), suggesting that OCT4 may be able to dynamically sample its target sites throughout the genome.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 1 and citations to Soufi et al., 2012, 2015.

claims.claim: Cooperation with BRG1 is required for more stable OCT4 binding.
claims.source: However, cooperation with BRG1 appears to be required for more stable OCT4 binding (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Enhanced OCT4 binding was observed during OCT4-SOX2-KLF4 reprogramming when BRG1 was included in the reprogramming cocktail.
claims.source: This general model is consistent with previous experiments that showed enhanced OCT4 binding during OCT4-SOX2-KLF4 reprogramming when BRG1 was included in the reprogramming cocktail (Singhal et al., 2010) and is in agreement with our observation that BRG1 is required for normal chromatin accessibility and OCT4 binding at otherwise inaccessible and inactive regulatory elements.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Singhal et al., 2010.

claims.claim: When ESCs are transitioned into epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs), OCT4 stably associates with a new set of previously inaccessible sites in a manner that appears to rely on co-binding of the EpiLC-specific transcription factor OTX2.
claims.source: In fitting with this possibility, when ESCs are transitioned into epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs), OCT4 stably associates with a new set of previously inaccessible sites in a manner that appears to rely on co-binding of the EpiLC-specific transcription factor OTX2 (Buecker et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Buecker et al., 2014 and Yang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: OCT4 is the only Yamanaka transcription factor that cannot be substituted for in iPSC reprogramming experiments.
claims.source: In agreement with these general ideas, OCT4 appears to be the only Yamanaka transcription factor that cannot be substituted for in iPSC reprogramming experiments, suggesting its pioneering activity is fundamental in establishing and maintaining the pluripotency network in concert with SOX2, KLF4 and c-Myc (Nakagawa et al., 2008; Sterneckert et al., 2012), perhaps due to its cooperation with BRG1 (Singhal et al., 2010; Esch et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakagawa et al., 2008; Sterneckert et al., 2012; Singhal et al., 2010; and Esch et al., 2013.

claims.claim: FoxA1 can stably bind its target sites and directly alter nucleosomal structure through steric disruption of histone:DNA contacts.
claims.source: While some pioneer factors, such as FoxA1, can stably bind their target sites and directly alter nucleosomal structure through steric disruption of histone:DNA contacts (Cirillo et al., 2002; Hatta and Cirillo, 2007; Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016), the extent to which other pioneer factors might exploit such a mechanism has yet to be fully addressed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cirillo et al., 2002; Hatta and Cirillo, 2007; and Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016.

claims.claim: OCT4 does not have an intrinsic chromatin opening activity, but requires cooperation with BRG1 to achieve this.
claims.source: In the case of OCT4, our observations establish that its capacity to support transcription factor binding and chromatin accessibility requires the chromatin remodeller BRG1. This suggests that unlike FoxA1, OCT4 does not have an intrinsic chromatin opening activity, but requires cooperation with BRG1 to achieve this.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on findings from Figures 3-5.

claims.claim: The pioneer factor GATA3 has similar dependency on BRG1 in creating accessible chromatin.
claims.source: Indeed, our work on OCT4 is generally consistent with and supported by recent work studying the pioneer factor GATA3 which appears to have similar dependency on BRG1 in creating accessible chromatin (Takaku et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Takaku et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Chromatin remodelling activity has been widely implicated in shaping nucleosome positioning and chromatin accessibility at target sites bound by other pioneer transcription factors.
claims.source: Furthermore, chromatin remodelling activity has been widely implicated in shaping nucleosome positioning and chromatin accessibility at target sites bound by other pioneer transcription factors (Hu et al., 2011; Sanalkumar et al., 2014; Ceballos-Chávez et al., 2015; Hainer and Fazzio, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2011; Sanalkumar et al., 2014; Ceballos-Chávez et al., 2015; and Hainer and Fazzio, 2015.

results.result: OCT4 binds predominantly to distal regulatory elements in mouse ESCs. ChIP-seq identified 15,920 high-confidence OCT4 binding sites, with 75% corresponding to distal regulatory elements (high H3K4me1/low H3K4me3) and only 6.8% to promoters (high H3K4me3/low H3K4me1).
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 provide converging evidence from ChIP-seq, motif enrichment, and histone modification analysis (Figures 1C-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) that OCT4 predominantly binds distal regulatory elements. The data are internally consistent and supported by appropriate controls and prior literature (C25).

results.result: OCT4 is required to maintain chromatin accessibility at its binding sites in ESCs. Following OCT4 depletion, 72% of OCT4 targets showed significant reductions in chromatin accessibility and increased nucleosome occupancy, with distal regulatory elements more affected than promoters. Many OCT4-bound sites became completely inaccessible and lacked accessibility in OCT4-negative cells and tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 are supported by ATAC-seq and nucleosome occupancy data (Figures 1E-J, Figure 1—figure supplements 2-3). The use of appropriate controls (Tn5 transposition control, multiple cell lines/tissues) and statistical thresholds (FDR < 0.05, fold change > 1.5) strengthens the conclusions. The pioneering role interpretation is well-supported.

results.result: OCT4 supports combinatorial transcription factor binding and pluripotency gene expression. Loss of OCT4 resulted in reduced SOX2 and NANOG binding at sites with decreased accessibility, which correlated with down-regulation of nearby pluripotency-associated genes. Down-regulated genes were significantly closer to OCT4 sites with reduced accessibility (median 16.2 kb) than those retaining accessibility (median 125.4 kb).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 are supported by integrated ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analyses (Figure 2). The correlation between accessibility loss, transcription factor binding reduction, and gene expression changes is well-documented. Gene ontology analysis confirms enrichment for pluripotency networks. The distance analysis (C37) provides spatial evidence linking OCT4 binding to gene regulation.

results.result: BRG1 is uniquely enriched at OCT4-dependent regulatory elements. Among nine chromatin remodeling complexes examined, only BRG1 showed appreciable correlation with OCT4-dependent chromatin accessibility. BRG1 was significantly enriched at OCT4-bound sites and OCT4-dependent ATAC peaks, with genome-wide co-localization of OCT4 and BRG1.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by systematic correlation analysis of multiple remodelers (Figure 3A) and BRG1 ChIP-seq data (Figures 3B-E). The comparative approach examining nine remodelers strengthens the specificity of the BRG1-OCT4 relationship. Genome-wide correlation analysis and published datasets provide additional support.

results.result: BRG1 is required for chromatin accessibility at OCT4 binding sites. Following BRG1 depletion, chromatin accessibility was reduced and nucleosome occupancy increased at the majority of OCT4 targets. Using stringent thresholds, 45% of OCT4-bound sites showed significantly reduced ATAC-seq signal, and 76% of OCT4-dependent sites were also BRG1-dependent. Loss of OCT4 or BRG1 resulted in similar reductions in chromatin accessibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by ATAC-seq and nucleosome occupancy data in BRG1-depleted cells (Figure 3I-J, Figure 3—figure supplements 1B-F). The use of both stringent thresholds and unbiased clustering approaches provides robust evidence. The similarity between OCT4 and BRG1 depletion effects supports their functional interdependence. Controls showing maintained protein levels and cell morphology are appropriate.

results.result: OCT4 recruits BRG1 and the BAF complex to its target sites. OCT4, BRG1, and BAF subunit SS18 co-localize within nucleosome-depleted regions at OCT4 sites. Following OCT4 depletion, BRG1 and SS18 binding was dramatically reduced at OCT4 targets but not at OCT4-free sites, and this loss correlated with reduced chromatin accessibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by high-resolution ChIP-seq analysis (Figure 4A-E). The specificity of BRG1/SS18 loss at OCT4-bound versus OCT4-free sites (C53) is critical evidence for recruitment. The correlation between BRG1/SS18 loss and accessibility loss (C54) supports functional significance. Protein level controls rule out indirect effects.

results.result: BRG1 is required to sustain transcription factor binding at OCT4 target sites. Following BRG1 removal, 60% of distal OCT4 targets showed significant reductions in OCT4 binding, while SOX2 and NANOG binding was reduced at 16.7% and 22.9% of sites, respectively. Even at the most affected sites, transcription factor binding was not completely lost, but cells could not maintain the nucleosome-depleted state.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by ChIP-seq data in BRG1-depleted cells (Figure 5A-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2). The differential effects on OCT4 versus SOX2/NANOG are interesting and well-documented. The observation that binding is reduced but not eliminated (C58) while nucleosome depletion is lost supports a model of BRG1-dependent maturation of pioneer binding events.

results.result: Gene expression changes following BRG1 depletion correlate with altered transcription factor binding at nearby regulatory elements. Genes associated with sites requiring BRG1 for OCT4 binding showed reduced expression, while genes near sites with unchanged or increased binding showed increased expression. Distal OCT4 sites near BRG1-dependent genes experienced the largest reductions in transcription factor binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by integrated RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analysis (Figure 5E-H, Figure 5—figure supplements 3-4). The correlation between binding changes and expression changes resolves previous inconsistencies in the literature. The bidirectional effects (both decreases and increases) are well-documented and mechanistically informative.

results.result: BRG1-dependency reflects temporal dynamics during reprogramming and development. Genes associated with BRG1-independent OCT4 binding were activated early during iPSC reprogramming, while BRG1-dependent genes were activated later. BRG1-dependent OCT4 sites were associated with genes expressed at later developmental stages and became accessible later during early mouse embryonic development.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by analysis of published reprogramming time-course data (Figure 6A), GREAT annotation (Figure 6B), and developmental ATAC-seq/DNase-seq data (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The convergence of evidence from multiple independent datasets (reprogramming and development) strengthens the conclusions. However, these are correlative analyses of published data rather than direct experimental tests.

results.result: OCT4 functions as a pioneer factor in ESCs by recruiting BRG1 to create accessible chromatin and support combinatorial transcription factor binding. This pioneering activity is required not only during reprogramming but also in the established pluripotent state to maintain the pluripotency-associated transcriptome.
results.evaluation: These summary claims (C66-C68) integrate findings from multiple experiments (Figures 1-5). The model is well-supported by the collective evidence showing OCT4 binding at inaccessible sites, BRG1 recruitment, chromatin accessibility changes, and effects on transcription factor binding and gene expression. The conclusion extends beyond reprogramming to the established pluripotent state.

results.result: Eukaryotic transcription factors face unique challenges compared to prokaryotic factors due to chromatin structure and shorter recognition sequences, requiring combinatorial binding and often pre-existing chromatin accessibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C11 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These provide necessary background context for understanding the significance of the experimental findings.

results.result: Pioneer transcription factors like FoxA1 can bind nucleosomal DNA and create accessible chromatin to support recruitment of non-pioneer factors. Mechanisms may involve structural mimicry of histones or recruitment of ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C18 represent established knowledge about pioneer factors supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential background for contextualizing the OCT4/BRG1 findings and comparing different pioneer factor mechanisms.

results.result: The Yamanaka factors (OCT4, SOX2, KLF4) can reprogram somatic cells to iPSCs and are proposed to act as pioneer factors that can bind nucleosome-occupied target sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 represent established knowledge about iPSC reprogramming supported by appropriate citations. This provides important context for studying OCT4 as a pioneer factor.

results.result: BRG1 is essential for ESC pluripotency, early embryonic development, and iPSC reprogramming efficiency. Prior proteomic studies suggested physical interaction between BRG1 and OCT4, and recent work showed BRG1 recruitment to pluripotency enhancers during reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44, C50, C55 represent prior knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context for the functional significance of the OCT4-BRG1 relationship and consistency with recent findings.

results.result: OCT4 may dynamically sample target sites through nucleosomal DNA binding, but requires BRG1 for stable binding. This model is consistent with enhanced OCT4 binding when BRG1 is included in reprogramming cocktails and OCT4's unique requirement in iPSC reprogramming. Co-binding factors like OTX2 may shape OCT4 binding in different cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 represent mechanistic interpretations and models based on the current findings integrated with prior literature. The model is well-supported by the experimental data and consistent with published observations, though some aspects remain speculative (e.g., dynamic sampling).

results.result: Unlike FoxA1, which can directly alter nucleosomal structure, OCT4 requires cooperation with the chromatin remodeler BRG1 to support transcription factor binding and chromatin accessibility. This dependency on chromatin remodelers may be a common feature of pioneer factors, as observed for GATA3 and others.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 compare OCT4's mechanism to other pioneer factors. The distinction from FoxA1 (C75) is well-supported by the experimental data showing BRG1 requirement. The comparison to GATA3 (C76) and broader generalization (C77) are supported by appropriate citations, though the extent of this mechanism across pioneer factors remains to be fully determined.
